hits.name: Sahil Bloom
hits.text: Underrated life advice: Keep proof that good things happen to you. Old photos. Kind messages. Positive feedback. Notes from great days. Whatever. Store them in a single place. Call it a Rainy Day Folder. Pop it open on a bad day and watch your mood turn. It's a free reset button.
hits.full_text: Underrated life advice: Keep proof that good things happen to you. Old photos. Kind messages. Positive feedback. Notes from great days. Whatever. Store them in a single place. Call it a Rainy Day Folder. Pop it open on a bad day and watch your mood turn. It's a free reset button.

hits.draft_en:
I started keeping a small pile of proof that good days happen.

A kind message. A page that went somewhere. A photo of the desk when it was quiet.

On the days that feel thin, I open it. Not to fix myself — just to remember the slow things already worked once.
hits.video_tip: 20–30s: open a drawer/notebook → flip past kind notes / one finished page / a quiet desk photo → close it gently. VO: 'Keep proof that good days happen. Open it when the day feels thin.'

x_posts.title: Clear pattern — trust follows consistency
x_posts.text:
Trust, for me, hasn't been a campaign.

It's been the quiet side effect of showing up the same way — same pen, same plain page, again tomorrow.

The pattern is the proof. One honest line, repeated.
x_posts.why: Mirrors Clear's climbing trust post; desk-scale.

x_posts.title: Naval/Ferriss pattern — long-term, as little as needed
x_posts.text:
I keep wanting to do more — more versions, more tabs, more "almost ready."

What I'm practicing instead: do as little as needed. The long-term version. One notebook. One decision I refuse to rush.

Not a bigger plan. Just the slow thing that still works in a year.

video_tip: 20–30s desk: open a notebook drawer → flip past a kind note / one finished page → set phone face-down → write one slow line. VO: 'Keep proof that good days happen. The long-term version is usually quieter.'
